items.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: and so Cecil called me and I was playing with his band

ctx.x: Well I was fresh in New York so I was open to everything. I had joined Cecil McBee’s band, I was playing also with Mickey Bass, you know, and I got the job with McBee’s band — well actually I first was with Jeanne Lee, that was the first New York job I ever

had. She passed away not too long ago. And Henry Threadgill had that job and he needed to go back to Chicago for something and he asked me to fill in for him and I did, and it was a great success and so they extended us another week. So I was with her. While I was doing that I was you know, just getting around New York, getting around, learning people, hanging out and meeting people. I then sat in with Mickey Bass and got hired to play. He had a month of Sundays and so after the Jeanne Lee thing, and so I was…
I guess so. And it probably hasn’t changed all that much, has it?

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: you performed at the Carnegie Hall in 1984 with Chico Freeman, just a duet.

ctx.x: Well let me put it this way: I’m my worst, I’ve been over the years, my worst critic. It continued. Until recently I never could appreciate what I’ve done. There’s always more and more that I could learn. And I don’t see that romantically, that’s realistic, you know, reality and so forth. But last summer my wife, knowing that I would return from the Conservatory at Boston at about 7:00, when I walked in there was this record going. And I said, “Wow, who is the bass player? If I could play like that, that’s where…
Nice. Well speaking of recognizing yourself and going back in your career, I came across an article that a critic, you performed at the Carnegie Hall in 1984 with Chico Freeman, just a duet.
